title: Hidden joy
hook: no soul knows what joy is kept hidden for them (32:17)

segments.voice: Yesterday, qiyam al-layl, and your line was up in the night. Did the alarm go off, and what did you do with the quiet? Day five hundred thirty-eight.

The best gifts are the ones you can't guess. A box handed over with a grin, and someone saying, don't shake it. Half the joy is not knowing. The other half is realizing, when you open it, that the giver knew you better than you thought. As-Sajdah has just described people getting out of bed in the dark to pray, unseen. And the very next verse says what's waiting for them. Or rather, it says something more interesting: that nobody knows.

Pickthall: "No soul knoweth what is kept hid for them of joy, as a reward for what they used to do." The phrase Pickthall translates joy is qurrat a'yun, literally, coolness of the eyes. It's an old Arabic idiom. In a hot land, coolness is relief; and many explain that tears of grief are hot, while tears of happiness are cool. So qurrat 'ayn is the thing that cools your eyes, that makes you deeply, quietly glad. The same phrase is used elsewhere in the Qur'an for a child, a spouse, the baby Musa returned to his mother. Here, it's kept hidden. Ukhfiya, concealed. A hadith in Bukhari brings this verse to life. The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ said that God says: I have prepared for My righteous servants what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and has never occurred to any human heart. And Abu Hurayra, who reported it, added: recite if you wish, no soul knows what is kept hidden for them. Some early commentators noticed a symmetry. The people in the verse before prayed in secret, at night, where no one could see. So their reward is secret too. A hidden deed, answered with a hidden joy. It's a kind of justice, and a kind of tenderness. The Qur'an gives many pictures of paradise: gardens, rivers, shade, fruit. This verse quietly says that all the pictures fall short. Whatever you imagine, it isn't that. It's more. And that leaves room for hope that doesn't need to be described to be real.
screen: `QURRAT A'YUN: COOLNESS OF THE EYES.` · `KEPT HIDDEN, UKHFIYA.` · `NO EYE HAS SEEN, NO EAR HAS HEARD.` · `A HIDDEN DEED, A HIDDEN JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do something good in secret. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of one good thing you could do today that nobody would ever know was you. Pay for someone's coffee and leave before they notice. Leave an anonymous kind note. Fix something broken at home before anyone sees it's broken. Give to a cause and tell no one. Picture doing it, and picture keeping it to yourself afterward, even when you're tempted to mention it. If you pray, you can offer it quietly. The bell holds the time.
Hidden joy. Qurrat a'yun, the coolness of the eyes, which As-Sajdah says is kept hidden for those who prayed unseen. Today's word.
Your line: joy kept hidden. Today, do the secret good you chose, and let it stay a secret. Day five hundred thirty-eight.

howItsDone: Many Muslims value hidden good deeds, such as secret charity and night prayer, and recite 32:17 alongside the hadith of what no eye has seen when speaking of paradise.

what it means: a reward kept hidden, beyond every picture, matched to deeds that were done unseen.
what a scholar hears: qurrat a'yun, coolness of eyes, with ukhfiya, concealed; and the hadith qudsi in Bukhari 4779, where Abu Hurayra recites this verse.

notes: Pickthall 32:17 quoted from memory; confirm wording.
The explanation of qurrat 'ayn (cool tears of joy, hot tears of grief) is a classical lexical explanation; another derives it from qarar, settling of the eye. Confirm.
The hidden-deed/hidden-reward symmetry is attributed to 'some early commentators' (e.g. reported from al-Hasan al-Basri); confirm.
